title: Character is the good
hookLine: for the Stoics only virtue is truly good, and health and money are extras
last: THE FENCE, THE SOIL, THE FRUIT.

cards: Imagine a wish list for your life. Most of us could fill it in without thinking: good health, enough money, maybe more than enough, a decent job, people who like us, a nice place to live.
Now a philosopher reads it over your shoulder and says: those are fine. Pleasant, even. But not one of them is actually good.
Only one thing is good, and it's not on your list. The Stoics said exactly that, and they meant it. Their word for it: arete.

teach.h: ARETE — EXCELLENCE, BEING GOOD AT IT.
teach.b: Arete is Greek, usually translated virtue, but the Greek word is wider and more practical. It means excellence, being good at what a thing is for. The arete of a knife is cutting well.
The arete of a horse is running well. So what is a human being for?

teach.h: A HUMAN'S JOB: REASON AND LIVE TOGETHER.
teach.b: The Stoics answered: we're the animals that reason and live together. Our excellence is reasoning well and treating each other well. In a word, character.
Then the bold claim: character is the only thing that's truly good, and bad character the only thing that's truly bad. Here's their test.

teach.h: ONLY WHAT CAN'T BE USED BADLY IS GOOD.
teach.b: A good thing should be good for you in every situation; it can never be used badly. Money fails: it can buy a meal for a hungry friend, or a bribe. Health fails: a strong body can help a neighbor move, or hurt someone.
Even cleverness can be used for a con. But wisdom? Justice?
Courage? The Stoics said these can't be turned to a bad use, because using things well is exactly what they are. Nobody does harm with too much justice.

That's why Seneca, writing to his friend Lucilius, keeps coming back to one idea: the only good is what is honorable, and a person is measured by that and nothing else. The Stoics weren't against health or money.
Tomorrow and the day after, you'll see they gladly preferred them. But they wouldn't stake a life on them.

teach.h: LOSE THE JOB, KEEP THE HONESTY.
teach.b: Lose your job and keep your honesty, and the Stoic says you've lost something pleasant and kept the thing that matters.
It's a demanding idea. It's also strangely freeing.

how: People who practice Stoicism often weigh a decision by asking what a person of good character would do, putting that above what they stand to gain or lose.

o: excellence: being good at what you're for
a prize given to the winner of a race
strict obedience to the rules of the gods

p: can be used well or badly

s: the Stoics said health and money are bad
they said those things aren't truly good or bad; they still preferred them.
arete means more than moral virtue: it means excellence
the excellence of anything is doing well what it's for.
for the Stoics, a true good can't be used badly
that's their test: money and health fail it, character passes.

games.q: a Greek asks: what is the arete of a knife?
games.why: arete is excellence at what a thing is for. for a knife, cutting; for a human, reasoning and living well together.

practice: Let three things you want from today come to mind: a task, a result, a feeling. Ask of each one: is this about what I get, or about who I am while I get it?
Finish the report, say, and be honest in it; move the character part to the top of the list and sit with that order.

wordCard.voice: Arete. Greek for excellence: being good at what you're for. For the Stoics, a human's excellence is good character, the only true good. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: excellence, virtue; used of knives and horses as well as people.

carryVoice: Your line: character first. How you act outranks what you get. That's day two hundred eighty-two.
